html.title: HTML Document Structure
html.content:
Give the browser page-wide information

The <head> contains metadata, the page title, and linked resources. The <body> contains the content people see and use.

html.title: Emphasis and Important Text
html.content:
Choose meaning, not appearance

<strong> marks importance and <em> adds emphasis. Browsers may style them boldly or in italics, but their meaning is what matters.
html.example:
Notice: The trail closes at dusk.

Please read the map before setting out.

html.title: Figures and Captions
html.content:
Keep media and its explanation together

Use <figure> to group self-contained media or an illustration with <figcaption> when it needs a caption.

html.title: Video Captions and Subtitles
html.content:
Make video understandable without sound

A <track> can associate a WebVTT captions file with a video. Captions include speech and meaningful sounds; provide accurate files and a visible way to enable controls.
html.example:
<video controls width="480">
  <source src="intro.mp4" type="video/mp4">
  <track src="intro.en.vtt" kind="captions" srclang="en" label="English">
  Your browser cannot play this video.
</video>

html.title: Expandable Details
html.content:
Show optional information on demand

The native <details> element creates a disclosure control. Put its visible label in <summary> and keep the extra information inside the details element.
html.example:
What should I bring?

Bring water, a map, and comfortable shoes.

html.title: Machine-Readable Time and Data
html.content:
Pair readable text with structured values

The <time> element can provide a machine-readable datetime value while showing a friendly date. The <data> element can associate a human label with a machine-readable value.

html.title: Responsive Images with Picture
html.content:
Offer an image that suits the situation

Use <picture> and <source> to let the browser select an image format or crop. Keep an <img> fallback with useful alternative text.

html.title: Page Titles and Descriptions
html.content:
Describe a page outside its body

A concise, unique <title> identifies a page in browser tabs and history. A meta description can summarize the page for search previews, though search engines may choose other text.
html.example:
<head>
  <title>Coastal Walks | Trail Notes</title>
  <meta name="description" content="Maps and advice for three coastal walks.">
</head>

html.title: Validate Input with Patterns
html.content:
Use built-in constraints carefully

The pattern attribute can constrain a text field with a regular expression. Explain the expected format in visible text; validation should help people correct input, not just reject it.
html.example: Enter six numbers, with no spaces.

html.title: Reusable Markup with Templates
html.content:
Keep reusable markup inert until needed

A <template> holds HTML that is not rendered immediately. JavaScript can clone its contents when creating repeated interface elements.

css.title: The Cascade and Specificity
css.content:
Understand which rule wins

When declarations conflict, the cascade considers origin, importance, specificity, and source order. Prefer simple selectors and remove obsolete rules rather than escalating specificity.

css.title: Inheritance and Initial Values
css.content:
Know which properties flow to children

Text-related properties such as color often inherit from a parent, while layout properties such as margin usually do not. Inspect computed styles when a value seems unexpected.

css.title: CSS Units and Relative Sizing
css.content:
Choose units for the job

Pixels can define fine details, while rem scales from the root font size and percentages relate to a containing box. Relative units help layouts adapt to user settings and viewport size.

css.title: Logical Properties
css.content:
Write layouts for different reading directions

Logical properties describe inline and block directions rather than physical left, right, top, or bottom. They make styles easier to reuse in right-to-left and vertical writing modes.

css.title: Overflow and Scrollable Content
css.content:
Decide what happens when content does not fit

The overflow properties control content that exceeds a box. Avoid hiding important content; when an area scrolls, ensure people can discover and operate it with a keyboard.

css.title: Transforms
css.content:
Change an element's visual position

Transforms can move, rotate, or scale an element without changing the normal document flow. Use them for visual effects, not as a substitute for arranging page layout.

css.title: CSS Functions and Clamp
css.content:
Make values respond within useful limits

calc() combines compatible values and clamp() sets a preferred value between a minimum and maximum. These functions can create fluid sizing without losing control at small or large screens.

css.title: Cascade Layers
css.content:
Organize rule precedence deliberately

Cascade layers let a stylesheet define priority groups up front. Later layers have priority over earlier layers for normal declarations, which can make large stylesheets easier to reason about.

css.title: Container Queries
css.content:
Respond to a component's available space

Container queries let a component adapt to the size of its container instead of the whole viewport. Declare a containment context, then query it for a layout change.

css.title: Respect Reduced-Motion Preferences
css.content:
Let people reduce animation

Some users ask their operating system for less motion. Use prefers-reduced-motion to remove or simplify nonessential animation while keeping important state changes understandable.

javascript.title: Scope and Block Bindings
javascript.content:
Keep variables close to where they are used

let and const are block-scoped. Use const by default, and choose let only when the binding needs reassignment.

javascript.title: Template Literals
javascript.content:
Build readable strings

Template literals use backticks and can interpolate expressions with ${...}. They are useful for combining values without a chain of concatenations.

javascript.title: Transform Arrays with Map and Filter
javascript.content:
Create a new array from existing data

map() transforms each item and filter() keeps items that pass a test. Both return new arrays and leave the original array unchanged.

javascript.title: Find an Item in an Array
javascript.content:
Look up one matching value

find() returns the first matching item, or undefined when there is no match. Use some() when you only need a yes-or-no answer.

javascript.title: Destructuring Values
javascript.content:
Extract values from arrays and objects

Destructuring assigns array items or object properties to local variables. It can make function parameters and data transformations easier to read.

javascript.title: Organize Code with Modules
javascript.content:
Share explicitly exported functionality

JavaScript modules let a file export values and another file import them. Keep module responsibilities focused, and use explicit imports to show dependencies.

javascript.title: Read and Write JSON
javascript.content:
Exchange data as text

JSON.stringify() converts supported JavaScript data to JSON text; JSON.parse() reads JSON text into values. Parsing can fail, so validate data from outside your program.

javascript.title: Save Small Values in the Browser
javascript.content:
Persist simple preferences

localStorage stores string values across browser sessions. Convert structured values to JSON, handle malformed stored data, and never store secrets in browser storage.

javascript.title: Handle Events on a Parent
javascript.content:
Use event delegation for repeated controls

A parent can handle events that bubble up from its children. Check the event target before acting, which is useful when list items are added dynamically.

javascript.title: Debounce Repeated Input
javascript.content:
Wait for a pause before running work

Debouncing delays an action until a sequence of rapid events pauses. It can reduce unnecessary search requests while someone is typing; always clear the pending timer when replacing it.

accessibility.title: Build a Clear Heading Structure
accessibility.content:
Make page sections easy to scan

Use headings to describe the content that follows and nest them in a meaningful order. Do not select a heading level just to get a particular font size; style it with CSS instead.
accessibility.example:
Community garden

Opening hours

Visit from sunrise to sunset.

accessibility.title: Write Links with Clear Purpose
accessibility.content:
Make destinations understandable

Link text should make sense when read on its own. Avoid vague labels like “click here”; include the destination or action without repeating surrounding text.

accessibility.title: Choose Buttons and Links Correctly
accessibility.content:
Match the control to its action

Use a link to navigate to another location and a button to perform an action on the current page. Native controls provide expected keyboard behavior and semantics.
accessibility.example: Browse events

accessibility.title: Write Useful Alternative Text
accessibility.content:
Describe an image's purpose

Alternative text should convey information needed to understand the page. Decorative images should generally have empty alt text so assistive technology can skip them; do not begin with “image of.”

accessibility.title: Announce Dynamic Updates
accessibility.content:
Make important updates available to assistive technology

A polite live region can announce status changes without moving focus. Keep announcements concise and avoid making frequently changing regions noisy.

accessibility.title: Make Dialogs Usable
accessibility.content:
Keep keyboard focus in the right place

Prefer the native <dialog> element for modal dialogs. Give the dialog a clear title, move focus into it when opened, and return focus to the opener when it closes.
accessibility.example:
Need help?

Contact the garden team for assistance.

accessibility.title: Connect Form Errors to Fields
accessibility.content:
Help people identify and correct errors

Describe what needs fixing in text and associate that message with its field. Keep the error visible and do not rely on color alone to communicate a problem.
accessibility.example: Enter an email address such as name@example.com.

accessibility.title: Keep Focus Order Predictable
accessibility.content:
Let keyboard users follow the page naturally

DOM order usually provides the most understandable focus order. Avoid positive tabindex values and do not remove focus outlines unless you provide an equally visible replacement.

accessibility.title: Make Controls Easy to Target
accessibility.content:
Give interactive controls room

Small or tightly packed controls can be difficult to activate, especially on touch screens. Provide comfortable spacing and follow current platform and accessibility guidance for target size.

accessibility.title: Build an Accessibility Check Routine
accessibility.content:
Combine tools with real interaction

Automated checks can find some issues, but they cannot confirm that a page is understandable. Test keyboard operation, zoom and text resizing, forms, and screen-reader output with representative content.

git.title: Inspect Changes and History
git.content:
Check the repository before acting

git status shows the working tree and staging area. git log shows recent commits; inspect both before preparing a change.

git.title: Stage Only the Changes You Intend
git.content:
Review what will go into a commit

Stage named files or individual hunks instead of blindly staging everything. Inspect the staged diff so unrelated work does not slip into the commit.

git.title: Amend the Most Recent Commit
git.content:
Correct a commit that has not been shared

git commit --amend updates the latest commit, often to add a missed file or improve its message. It changes history, so avoid amending commits that others already depend on.

git.title: Ignore Generated and Local Files
git.content:
Keep temporary files out of version control

Patterns in .gitignore prevent untracked files from appearing as candidates for staging. Ignoring a file does not remove it if Git already tracks it.

git.title: Restore a File Safely
git.content:
Discard only changes you have reviewed

git restore can restore a working-tree file or unstage a staged file. Review the diff first: restoring a file discards changes in that scope.
git.example:
git diff -- src/app.js
git restore -- src/app.js

git restore --staged -- README.md

git.title: Temporarily Stash Work
git.content:
Set aside unfinished changes

A stash saves selected working-tree changes so you can switch tasks. Name stashes clearly and inspect them before applying or dropping them.

git.title: Rebase a Branch onto Updated Work
git.content:
Replay local commits on a newer base

Rebasing moves a branch's commits onto another starting point, producing a linear history. Resolve conflicts carefully; do not rewrite shared history without coordinating with collaborators.
git.example:
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main

git.title: Apply One Commit to Another Branch
git.content:
Reuse a focused change

git cherry-pick applies the changes from an existing commit onto the current branch. Use it for a specific fix rather than copying files by hand.
git.example:
git switch release
git cherry-pick abc1234

git.title: Tag a Release
git.content:
Mark an important point in history

Tags give a stable name to a commit, often for a release. Annotated tags include metadata and a message, making them suitable for published versions.
git.example:
git tag -a v1.2.0 -m "Release 1.2.0"
git show v1.2.0
git push origin v1.2.0

git.title: Find a Bug with Git Bisect
git.content:
Narrow down when a regression began

git bisect performs a binary search through commit history. Mark a known good and bad commit, test each suggested revision, and finish the session when the culprit is identified.
git.example:
git bisect start
git bisect bad
git bisect good v1.0.0
# Test each revision and mark it:
git bisect good
git bisect bad
git bisect reset

apis.title: Understand REST Resources
apis.content:
Think in resources and representations

REST-style APIs expose resources through URLs and use HTTP methods to express common operations. Consistent resource names and response shapes make an API easier to use.

apis.title: Send Request Headers
apis.content:
Include metadata with a request

Headers carry information such as content type and authorization. Send only headers required by the API, and do not expose private tokens in client-side code.

apis.title: Send JSON to an API
apis.content:
Describe a request body clearly

When sending JSON, serialize the value and set the Content-Type header. A server should validate the request body rather than trusting its shape.

apis.title: Paginate Large Results
apis.content:
Request manageable pages of data

Pagination limits how much data a response returns at once. Follow the API's documented page or cursor format, and use its next-page information instead of guessing.

apis.title: Respond to Rate Limits
apis.content:
Handle requests that are temporarily limited

An API may return status 429 when a client sends too many requests. Respect documented retry information and use bounded backoff instead of retrying continuously.

apis.title: Understand Cross-Origin Requests
apis.content:
Know when browsers allow a request

Browsers enforce the same-origin policy. A server can opt into cross-origin access with CORS response headers; client code cannot bypass that policy by changing its request.
apis.example:
fetch('https://api.example.test/items')
  .then(response => response.json())
  .then(items => console.log(items))
  .catch(error => console.error('Network or CORS error:', error));

apis.title: Use HTTP Caching
apis.content:
Reuse responses when they are still valid

Caching headers such as Cache-Control guide browsers and intermediaries. For frequently changing data, validators such as ETags can help check whether a representation changed.

apis.title: Validate API Response Shapes
apis.content:
Check data before relying on it

A successful HTTP response can still contain unexpected data. Confirm required fields and types at the boundary before using the response throughout an application.

apis.title: Cancel an Unneeded Request
apis.content:
Stop work when a request is no longer relevant

AbortController can cancel a fetch, such as when a user changes search terms or leaves a page. Handle aborts separately from other request errors when appropriate.

apis.title: Plan for API Versions
apis.content:
Change an API without surprising clients

Versioning and clear deprecation policies help clients adapt to breaking changes. Prefer compatible additions when possible and document how long older versions remain available.

projects.title: Choose an Audience and Goal
projects.content:
Decide who the project helps

A useful project starts with a specific audience and a clear problem. Write one sentence describing what a person should be able to do after using it.
projects.example:
Audience: people sharing a community garden.
Goal: find the next open volunteer session.
Success: a visitor can locate date, time, and signup details.

projects.title: Define a Small First Version
projects.content:
Separate essentials from future ideas

List the smallest set of features that delivers the main value. Keep optional improvements in a later list so the first version can be completed and tested.
projects.example:
First version:
- Show three upcoming sessions
- Display date and location
- Link to a signup form

Later: filters, reminders, and member profiles.

projects.title: Sketch the Main Screen
projects.content:
Plan the page before polishing it

A quick sketch helps establish hierarchy and identify missing content. Focus on the main task, readable sections, and a clear next action.
projects.example:
[Site title]
[Upcoming sessions]
  Session name | Date | Location
  [View details]
[How to participate]
[Contact information]

projects.title: Prepare Realistic Content
projects.content:
Design for the content people will actually see

Use realistic names, lengths, and edge cases rather than repeated placeholder text. Include empty, long, and missing values so the layout is tested beyond its ideal state.

projects.title: Build a Responsive Layout
projects.content:
Start with a flexible page structure

Use normal document flow and flexible layout tools before adding breakpoints. Test at narrow and wide widths, and avoid fixed dimensions that clip content.

projects.title: Add One Useful Interaction
projects.content:
Make the main action work end to end

Choose an interaction that advances the project's goal, such as filtering a list or submitting a form. Give clear feedback for success, errors, and empty results.

projects.title: Review Project Accessibility
projects.content:
Check the interface with different ways of interacting

Use semantic controls, visible focus, clear labels, and sufficient text contrast. Try every interaction with a keyboard and confirm status messages are understandable.
projects.example: 3 sessions shown

projects.title: Collect Useful Feedback
projects.content:
Ask people to try a real task

Observe someone using the project without explaining every step. Ask what they expected, note where they hesitated, and prioritize fixes that block the main goal.
projects.example:
Task: Find the next session near the north beds.
Observe: Where does the tester look first?
Ask afterward: What was unclear?
Improve: Fix the biggest obstacle, then test again.

projects.title: Check the Finished Project
projects.content:
Verify common states before sharing

Check links, forms, console errors, layout sizes, and content with realistic data. Re-test the main task after changes so a polish pass does not introduce regressions.
projects.example:
Project review:
[ ] Main task works
[ ] Links lead to the right place
[ ] Narrow screen remains usable
[ ] Keyboard focus is visible
[ ] Empty and error states make sense

projects.title: Plan the Next Iteration
projects.content:
Make improvements manageable

Record known limitations and the next most valuable improvement. Small, testable iterations are easier to maintain than a large list of unfinished features.
projects.example:
Next iteration:
1. Add a location filter.
2. Test it with keyboard and touch.
3. Ask a visitor to find a session.
4. Keep or revise the design based on what happened.

roadmap.title: Practice Meaningful HTML Structure
roadmap.content:
Move from tags to page structure

Build a page with a clear title, headings, landmarks, links, and a small list. Check that the document still makes sense when styles are removed.

roadmap.title: Practice Flexible CSS Layout
roadmap.content:
Arrange content without fixed page assumptions

Use Flexbox for a row or column of related items and Grid for two-dimensional arrangements. Let the layout respond to available space instead of relying on exact viewport sizes.

roadmap.title: Improve Readability with Typography
roadmap.content:
Make text comfortable to read

Choose a readable line length, line height, and consistent type scale. Test longer paragraphs and larger text settings to ensure the design remains usable.

roadmap.title: Represent Interface Data
roadmap.content:
Keep content and rendering separate

Store repeated content as data, then render it from one template. This makes updates consistent and helps you handle empty or filtered results.

roadmap.title: Connect a Form to Page Behavior
roadmap.content:
Read and validate user input

Listen for the form's submit event, prevent navigation only when you handle the submission, and report errors in a clear place. Keep native HTML constraints where they help.

roadmap.title: Use Git for Small Checkpoints
roadmap.content:
Save progress in focused commits

Make commits that describe one coherent change. Review diffs before committing and use a separate branch when experimenting or collaborating.
roadmap.example:
git switch -c add-event-filter
git status --short
git add public/
git diff --cached
git commit -m "Add event list filtering"

roadmap.title: Debug with a Reproducible Check
roadmap.content:
Turn a bug report into a testable problem

Write down the steps, expected result, and actual result. Reproduce the issue with the browser console and inspect the smallest relevant part of the code.
roadmap.example:
Problem: filtering shows no results for uppercase input.
Expected: matching should ignore capitalization.
Check: compare normalized query and title.
Fix: normalize both values before matching.

roadmap.title: Check Page Performance Basics
roadmap.content:
Keep the first experience responsive

Use appropriately sized images, avoid unnecessary scripts, and test the page on a slower connection. Measure before optimizing so effort targets a real bottleneck.

roadmap.title: Prepare a Site for Deployment
roadmap.content:
Verify configuration and production behavior

Check that static paths, environment configuration, and error handling work outside your development machine. Keep secrets out of the repository and review the deployed version after release.
roadmap.example:
Release checklist:
- Build succeeds from a clean checkout
- Required environment values are configured
- No secret values are committed
- Deployed homepage and links work

roadmap.title: Choose a Next Learning Goal
roadmap.content:
Continue with a focused project

Pick one skill that your current project needs, then build a small feature using it. Explain what you learned and keep the result available as a portfolio example.
roadmap.example:
Project idea: a searchable reading list
Practice: semantic forms, array filtering, and local storage
Finish: document setup, decisions, and known limitations

project-challenges.title: Challenge 6: Build an Event Page
project-challenges.content:
Help visitors understand and join an event

Create an event page with date, location, schedule, and a clear signup action. Use semantic sections, responsive layout, and accessible link and form labels.

Stretch goal

Add a schedule that remains readable on a narrow screen.
project-challenges.example:
Neighborhood clean-up

Saturday, 9:00 AM · Meet at the library

Plan

  1. Check in
  2. Choose a route
  3. Return supplies
Sign up to volunteer

project-challenges.title: Challenge 7: Build a Recipe Card
project-challenges.content:
Present a recipe people can follow

Show ingredients, preparation steps, time, and servings. Use a meaningful heading structure and an ordered list for steps.

Stretch goal

Add a serving-size control and update the ingredient amounts.
project-challenges.example:
Simple tomato salad

Prep: 10 minutes · Serves 2

Ingredients

  • 3 ripe tomatoes
  • 1 tbsp olive oil

Method

  1. Slice the tomatoes.
  2. Drizzle with oil and serve.

project-challenges.title: Challenge 8: Build a Weather Card
project-challenges.content:
Design a useful weather summary

Create a card with location, current conditions, temperature, and a short forecast. Make the information understandable without relying on an icon or color alone.

Stretch goal

Load sample data asynchronously and show loading and error states.
project-challenges.example:
Today's weather · Lakeside

☀ Sunny, 22°C

High 24°C · Low 16°C

project-challenges.title: Challenge 9: Build a Reading List
project-challenges.content:
Track books a reader wants to finish

Display a list of books and let the reader mark one complete. Keep the controls labeled and show a useful message when the list is empty.

Stretch goal

Add a filter for unread books.

project-challenges.title: Challenge 10: Build an FAQ
project-challenges.content:
Make answers easy to find

Organize common questions into clear categories and write concise answers. Use native disclosure elements so visitors can expand answers with keyboard or pointer.

Stretch goal

Add a search field that filters questions without hiding the page title.
project-challenges.example:
Frequently asked questions

Is the workshop free?

Yes. Registration is free, but space is limited.

project-challenges.title: Challenge 11: Build a Countdown
project-challenges.content:
Show time remaining until an event

Create a countdown with an explicit target date and clear units. Handle the state after the event begins, and avoid announcing every second to assistive technology.

Stretch goal

Allow the visitor to choose a target date.

project-challenges.title: Challenge 12: Build a Color Picker
project-challenges.content:
Let visitors explore a color value

Use a labeled color input and display its current value as text. Ensure the preview has enough contrast and that color is not the only signal.

Stretch goal

Show a copy button and confirmation status.
project-challenges.example:
<label for="accent">Choose an accent color</label>
<input id="accent" type="color" value="#176b5b">
<output id="color-value">#176b5b</output>

project-challenges.title: Challenge 13: Build a Tabbed Panel
project-challenges.content:
Organize related content into panels

Build tabs with clear labels, keyboard support, and a visible selected state. Use the tab roles and relationships correctly, or choose simpler disclosure links if custom keyboard behavior is out of scope.

Stretch goal

Support arrow-key movement between tabs.
project-challenges.example: Planting season begins in spring.

project-challenges.title: Challenge 14: Build an Expense List
project-challenges.content:
Summarize a small set of expenses

Show each expense with a description and amount, then calculate a total. Use appropriate number formatting and handle an empty list.

Stretch goal

Let people add and remove entries with clear form labels.

project-challenges.title: Challenge 15: Build a Contact Form
project-challenges.content:
Collect a message with helpful feedback

Create labeled name, email, and message fields. Add suitable browser validation, explain required fields, and show a clear confirmation after a valid submission.

Stretch goal

Provide a summary of validation errors and focus the first invalid field.
project-challenges.example:
<form>
  <label for="name">Name</label>
  <input id="name" name="name" autocomplete="name" required>
  <label for="message">Message</label>
  <textarea id="message" name="message" required></textarea>
  <button>Send message</button>
</form>

quiz.title: HTML Structure Quick Quiz
quiz.content:
Check your HTML foundations

What belongs in the <head>? Which element represents the main content of a page? How would you make an image decorative for assistive technology?

Answers

Metadata and linked resources belong in the head; use <main> for primary content; a decorative image usually uses alt="".

quiz.title: HTML Forms Quick Quiz
quiz.content:
Review form semantics

How does a label connect to an input? Which input type helps validate an email address? What does required do?

Answers

Match the label's for with the input's id; use type="email"; required asks the browser to prevent an empty submission.

quiz.title: CSS Cascade Quick Quiz
quiz.content:
Review how styles are chosen

Which is more specific: a class selector or an element selector? Does margin normally inherit? What should you inspect when a style surprises you?

Answers

A class selector is more specific; margin normally does not inherit; inspect the cascade and computed styles in developer tools.

quiz.title: CSS Layout Quick Quiz
quiz.content:
Review responsive layout choices

When is Grid useful? Which property creates space between flex or grid items? Why can a fixed-width layout fail on a small screen?

Answers

Grid is useful for rows and columns; gap sets spacing; a fixed width can overflow the available viewport.

quiz.title: JavaScript Values Quick Quiz
quiz.content:
Review variables and values

When should you use const? What does typeof help inspect? What is the value of an object property that does not exist?

Answers

Use const when the binding will not be reassigned; typeof reports a value's type category; a missing object property evaluates to undefined.

quiz.title: JavaScript Arrays Quick Quiz
quiz.content:
Review common array methods

Which method transforms every item into a new array? Which method keeps items that pass a test? What does find() return when nothing matches?

Answers

Use map() to transform; filter() to select; find() returns undefined when there is no match.

quiz.title: JavaScript Async Quick Quiz
quiz.content:
Review promises and fetch

What does await do inside an async function? Does fetch reject for an HTTP 404 response? How can code check whether a response succeeded?

Answers

Await pauses that async function until a promise settles; fetch usually resolves for HTTP errors; check response.ok.

quiz.title: Accessibility Quick Quiz
quiz.content:
Review inclusive interaction

How can you make a decorative image skippable? What should a visible keyboard focus indicator do? Why should errors not be indicated by color alone?

Answers

Use empty alt text for decorative images; show a clear focus outline; pair color with text or another non-color cue.

quiz.title: Git Quick Quiz
quiz.content:
Review everyday Git workflow

What does staging choose? Which command displays the staged diff? Why should shared commits not be casually rewritten?

Answers

Staging selects changes for the next commit; use git diff --cached; rewriting shared history can disrupt collaborators' work.
quiz.example:
git status --short
git add src/app.js
git diff --cached
git commit -m "Describe the change"

quiz.title: Web Foundations Mixed Quiz
quiz.content:
Connect HTML, CSS, and JavaScript

Which language describes page structure? Which language styles it? Which language can respond to interaction? Why should a button action use a real button element?

Answers

HTML describes structure, CSS styles it, and JavaScript adds behavior; a native button has built-in keyboard and accessibility behavior.

sql.title: Work with NULL Values
sql.content:
Represent missing or unknown data

NULL is not equal to an ordinary value, including another NULL. Use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL to test for missing values.

sql.title: Create Conditional Values with CASE
sql.content:
Return a value based on conditions

CASE evaluates conditions in order and returns the first matching result. Include an ELSE branch when you want an explicit fallback.
sql.example:
SELECT name,
  CASE
    WHEN score >= 80 THEN 'high'
    WHEN score >= 50 THEN 'medium'
    ELSE 'low'
  END AS score_band
FROM results;

sql.title: Select Distinct Values
sql.content:
Remove duplicate result rows

DISTINCT removes duplicate combinations from the selected columns. It is not a substitute for understanding why a join or source table produces duplicates.

sql.title: Search Text with LIKE
sql.content:
Match simple text patterns

LIKE uses % for any number of characters and _ for one character. Case sensitivity depends on the database and collation.

sql.title: Filter and Group by Dates
sql.content:
Work with date ranges deliberately

Use the date and time types supported by your database and compare a clear start and end. Half-open ranges avoid ambiguity at the next period boundary.
sql.example:
SELECT created_at, total
FROM orders
WHERE created_at >= '2026-10-01'
  AND created_at < '2026-11-01';

sql.title: Connect Tables with Foreign Keys
sql.content:
Protect relationships between records

A foreign key requires a value to reference a row in another table. Choose update and delete behavior that preserves the data rules your application needs.

sql.title: Enforce Unique Values
sql.content:
Keep identifiers from being duplicated

A UNIQUE constraint makes the database enforce a rule even when multiple clients write data. Decide how your database treats multiple NULL values before relying on that behavior.

sql.title: Create a View
sql.content:
Name a reusable query

A view presents the result of a query as a named database object. It can simplify repeated reads, but it does not automatically make a query faster.

sql.title: Understand Index Trade-Offs
sql.content:
Use indexes to support common lookups

Indexes can speed up filtering and joins, but they consume storage and add work to writes. Use query plans and workload evidence to decide which indexes are useful.
sql.example:
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_date
ON orders(customer_id, created_at);

sql.title: Use Parameters in SQL Queries
sql.content:
Separate query structure from input values

Parameterized queries let the database treat user input as data rather than executable SQL. Use the placeholder syntax supported by your database driver.
sql.example:
SELECT id, name
FROM customers
WHERE email = ?;

-- Bind the email value through the database driver's parameter API.

express.title: Return JSON Responses
express.content:
Send a consistent representation

Use res.json() for JSON responses so Express serializes the value and sets an appropriate content type. Keep response shapes predictable for clients.

express.title: Choose an HTTP Status Code
express.content:
Describe the result of a request

Use status codes to communicate whether a request succeeded, created a resource, lacked a required resource, or was invalid. Send a concise response body that helps the client recover.

express.title: Mount Routers under a Prefix
express.content:
Organize endpoints by feature

Express routers can group related routes and middleware. Mount a router at a prefix to keep route modules focused and avoid repeating the same path segment.

express.title: Understand Middleware Order
express.content:
Register middleware before routes that need it

Express runs middleware in registration order. A middleware function must either end the response or call next(); error middleware uses a separate signature and flow.

express.title: Validate Route Parameters
express.content:
Reject malformed input early

Route parameters and query values arrive as strings. Validate their expected format and range before using them to read or change application data.

express.title: Handle Errors in One Place
express.content:
Keep error responses consistent

Pass unexpected errors to Express error-handling middleware. Log useful details on the server, but avoid exposing stack traces or sensitive implementation information to clients.

express.title: Add a Not-Found Handler
express.content:
Respond when no route matches

A not-found middleware runs after registered routes when none has ended the response. Return a clear 404 without confusing it with an unexpected server error.

express.title: Understand Cookies and Sessions
express.content:
Use browser cookies with care

Cookies can carry session identifiers, but session design requires secure generation, expiration, and appropriate cookie flags. Do not store sensitive application data directly in a cookie.

express.title: Configure Static File Serving
express.content:
Serve public assets from a known directory

express.static() exposes files under a directory. Choose the directory intentionally and mount it at a predictable URL prefix.

express.title: Add a Health Check Endpoint
express.content:
Report whether a service is responding

A health endpoint gives deployment systems a simple way to check service availability. Keep its response lightweight and do not include credentials or internal diagnostic details.

react.title: Group Elements with Fragments
react.content:
Return related elements without extra markup

React fragments group multiple elements without adding a wrapper to the DOM. Use the short syntax for simple groups and the named Fragment when a keyed fragment is needed.

react.title: Render UI Conditionally
react.content:
Show the interface for the current state

Use normal JavaScript conditions to select what a component renders. Make loading, empty, success, and error states explicit instead of leaving users with a blank region.

react.title: Work with Controlled Inputs
react.content:
Keep an input value in React state

A controlled input receives its value from state and updates that state in an event handler. This makes the current value available for validation and conditional UI.

react.title: Share State Between Components
react.content:
Lift shared state to a common parent

When sibling components need the same changing value, place that state in their closest shared parent and pass values and callbacks as props.

react.title: Calculate Values from Existing State
react.content:
Avoid storing information you can derive

Compute values such as filtered lists from props and state during rendering when the calculation is straightforward. Duplicated state can become inconsistent.

react.title: Clean Up Effects
react.content:
Release resources when an effect is replaced

Effects that subscribe to events, start timers, or connect to external systems should return a cleanup function. React runs cleanup before the effect is set up again and when the component unmounts.

react.title: Share Values with Context
react.content:
Provide data to a subtree

Context is useful for values needed by many descendants, such as a theme. Keep context focused; values that change often can cause many consumers to re-render.

react.title: Memoize Only When It Helps
react.content:
Optimize measured rendering work

Memoization can avoid repeated calculations or renders, but it adds complexity and has its own cost. Start with clear components and profile before adding memoization.

react.title: Handle Rendering Errors
react.content:
Show a fallback when a subtree fails

Error boundaries catch rendering errors in descendant components and display a fallback UI. They do not catch every error, such as failures inside event handlers or arbitrary asynchronous callbacks.

react.title: Test Component Behavior
react.content:
Test what a person can observe

Component tests should focus on visible behavior: labels, content, and responses to interaction. Prefer accessible queries and avoid tests that depend on private implementation details.

dart.title: Build Strings with Interpolation
dart.content:
Include values in readable strings

Dart string interpolation inserts a variable with $name or an expression with ${...}. Use it to avoid hard-to-read concatenation.

dart.title: Choose a Collection Type
dart.content:
Store groups of values appropriately

A List is ordered, a Set stores unique values, and a Map associates keys with values. Pick the collection that matches how data will be accessed.

dart.title: Transform and Filter Lists
dart.content:
Work with list elements declaratively

Collection methods such as where and map can filter and transform values. Convert an iterable to a list when you need a concrete list result.

dart.title: Represent Fixed Choices with Enums
dart.content:
Give a closed set of choices clear names

Enums represent a finite set of named values. They are safer and clearer than using unrelated strings for states such as loading, success, and failure.

dart.title: Add Helpers with Extension Methods
dart.content:
Define focused behavior for existing types

Extension methods add callable helpers to a type without changing that type. Keep extensions small and avoid names that make behavior surprising.

dart.title: Use Named Parameters
dart.content:
Make function calls self-describing

Named parameters make arguments easier to identify at a call site. Use required for values that must be supplied and defaults for optional values with a sensible fallback.

dart.title: Use Factory Constructors
dart.content:
Control how an object is created

A factory constructor can return an existing instance, create a subtype, or parse data before building an object. Use a generative constructor when it simply initializes a new instance.

dart.title: Listen to a Stream
dart.content:
Handle a sequence of asynchronous values

A Stream can emit multiple values over time. Subscribe with a listener or use asynchronous iteration, and handle errors and cancellation for long-lived streams.

dart.title: Convert JSON into Dart Data
dart.content:
Parse and validate structured text

The dart:convert library can decode JSON into Dart values. Check the structure and types before using decoded values, especially when data comes from outside the application.

dart.title: Prefer Immutable Data
dart.content:
Make values easier to reason about

Use final for fields that should not be reassigned and immutable collections when callers should not mutate them. Clear ownership reduces accidental shared-state changes.

flutter.title: Add an App Bar and Actions
flutter.content:
Give a screen a clear top-level action

An AppBar can show a title and actions related to the current screen. Use descriptive tooltips for icon-only buttons.

flutter.title: Work with Layout Constraints
flutter.content:
Let parent constraints guide child sizes

Flutter layout passes constraints from parents to children and sizes back up the tree. Use flexible widgets such as Expanded and Flexible when children share available space.

flutter.title: Use the App Color Scheme
flutter.content:
Keep component colors consistent

Define an app color scheme through the theme instead of repeating unrelated color constants. Use foreground and background pairs that remain readable in each theme.

flutter.title: Load Images from Assets
flutter.content:
Declare and display bundled images

Assets must be declared in the Flutter project configuration before they can be loaded. Provide dimensions or constraints so images fit the intended layout.

flutter.title: Use Keys in Dynamic Lists
flutter.content:
Help Flutter identify changing list items

Keys preserve the identity of widgets when items are inserted, removed, or reordered. Use a stable key derived from each item's identity rather than its current position.

flutter.title: Show Loading, Success, and Error States
flutter.content:
Represent every stage of asynchronous work

People need feedback while data loads and a recovery path if it fails. Keep loading, error, empty, and success states visually distinct and easy to understand.

flutter.title: Manage Text Editing Controllers
flutter.content:
Read and release text field state

A TextEditingController provides access to a field's current value. Create it in the appropriate state object and dispose of it when that state is removed.

flutter.title: Return a Result from a Screen
flutter.content:
Send a selected value back to the caller

A pushed route can return a result when it is popped. Await the navigation result and handle cancellation as well as a selected value.

flutter.title: Label Icon-Only Controls
flutter.content:
Provide a spoken name for an icon action

An icon may communicate appearance but not its action to everyone. Add a tooltip and semantic label to icon-only controls, and ensure the tap target is comfortable.

flutter.title: Write a Widget Test
flutter.content:
Verify a screen's visible behavior

Widget tests can pump a widget tree, interact with controls, and assert on rendered output. Test outcomes that matter to a user rather than private implementation details.
